Sure. Here’s something I wrote just because—free, loose, and a little dreamy.

---

Some mornings arrive like they’ve been rehearsed: the light gets poured in at exactly the right angle, dust hangs in the air as if it’s waiting to be named, and the world behaves as though it knows the rules. On those days, you can almost believe in order—believe that everything has a place and that the day will politely stay in its lane.

Other mornings are messier. They wake you up mid-thought, when your mind is still wearing the night like a coat that doesn’t fit. The first thing you hear is not a sound but a feeling: the sense that something is slipping, not dramatically, not like a disaster—just the way a thread comes loose from a hem. You try to catch it with your attention, but it keeps unraveling into smaller and smaller strands, none of them quite sharp enough to see.

I think that’s why people talk about beginnings as if they’re gentle. They aren’t. Beginnings are negotiations. They ask you to trade certainty for momentum. They say: “Walk with us now—don’t stand there waiting for the world to explain itself.”

And the funny thing is, you do. You put on your shoes, you reach for your keys, you open the door to a day you cannot control. Even when you’re afraid, you still move. Not because you’ve solved your fear, but because fear is only one passenger among many, and the body insists on going forward anyway.

Sometimes you notice small mercies that don’t announce themselves. A stranger lets you merge without looking up. The coffee tastes better than it has any right to. You remember a line from a book you loved years ago, and suddenly you’re twelve again—not in a sentimental way, but in a way that restores your belief in your own capacity to feel. You realize you’re not falling apart; you’re being rebuilt with different materials.

The day will end either way. That’s one of the contracts we sign without reading: the light will eventually retreat, the noise will soften, your thoughts will grow quiet at the edges. And when evening comes, you’ll do the human thing—review the hours like they were evidence in a trial. You’ll decide what mattered, what didn’t, and what you wish you’d said.

Then, somehow, you’ll sleep.

And in sleep, the mind practices being infinite for a few hours. It stitches together images that don’t belong together. It holds conversations with people you haven’t seen in a long time. It rehearses alternate lives. In the morning, some of that vanishes, but some of it stays behind like a scent on a jacket—proof that something in you has been working even while you weren’t watching.

That’s what I want to believe: that even when the day feels unremarkable, something is happening. Even when you feel stuck, you’re changing in increments too small to measure. Even when you can’t see the plot, the story is still moving.

Not toward perfection. Not toward a predetermined happy ending.

Just toward the next moment—where you’ll get to decide, again, whether to walk through the door.

---
